meaning.text: His name is said to be derived from kost', a bone, whence comes a verb meaning to ossify or grow hard as bone or stone, a figurative expression for 'to freeze'.
Some mythologists derive the name from kost', a bone, either because he is bony of limb or because he produces an effect akin to freezing or petrifaction.
He is called 'Immortal' or 'The Deathless' because of his superiority to the ordinary laws of existence.
In Old Slavonic texts the word koshch' occurs only in the sense of dry, lean, thin of body, and is evidently closely related to the word kost', bone.

appearance.text: Sometimes he is described as altogether serpent-like in form.
Sometimes he seems to be of a mixed nature, partly human and partly serpent.
In some of the stories he is apparently framed after the fashion of a man.

scene.text: In a Russian story he is found in a forbidden chamber, hung up and bound with twelve chains.
He says he has hung there without drinking for ten years.

In another version the hero finds him in the forbidden chamber in a cauldron amid flames, boiling in pitch, where he says he has been for fifteen years, lured there by the beauty of Anastasia the Fair.
In a further version he is found in the forbidden chamber seated on a horse which is chained to a cauldron.

behavior_habitat.text: In the stories he keeps beautiful princesses in imprisonment until his spell is broken and his power overthrown.
Sometimes he suddenly carries off a hero's mother, sometimes the hero's wife, and keeps her prisoner.
In the tales he plays the same part as the snake: a miserly guardian of treasures and a dangerous abductor of beautiful maidens, hostile to the heroes.
He and the snake freely replace each other, so that one variant of a tale has the snake and another has Koshchei.
Like the devouring snakes, he smells 'the scent of the Russian spirit'.
A folk tale ascribes to him self-playing gusli that play so skilfully that anyone who hears them listens to the point of death.
In a Polish version of the 'Sleeping Beauty' he carries off the princess and throws her and all the inhabitants of her father's kingdom into a magic slumber.
In that Polish version the rescuer conquers him and seizes his magic gusli, and at their music the sleepers awake.
When given water he drinks his fill, recovers his lost strength, bursts his chains and flies away, carrying off the queen.
When the prince shifts the egg that holds his death from hand to hand, he rushes wildly from side to side of the room.

dealing_with_it.text: His prisoner is held until the hero finds out in what place his 'death' can be discovered.
He is generally induced to make some such revelation as that his death lies in an egg, in a duck, in a hare, in a casket under an oak; when the egg is found and broken, he dies.
In one story he first claims his death is in a besom, then in the fence round the house, and his captive adorns each with gold before he tells the truth.
Different versions give different animals in the chain that secures his life, the last link being an egg or a stone inside an egg.
In one variant the hero is helped in his search for the fatal egg by the Thunder, the Wind and the Hail.
Sometimes he cannot be killed except by one substance.
In one telling he is killed by a blow on the forehead struck with the egg.
Having taken the wondrous egg, the prince throws it at Koshchei's forehead and he dies at once.
In the Marya Morevna story a magic steed fells him with a kick on the forehead.
In charms an incantation against Koshchei-yadun is still pronounced.

rationale.text: The verified entry records Koshchei for Russians, in Afanasyev's account of Russian folk tradition and in Ralston's Russian stories.
It records him for Poles through a Polish version of the 'Sleeping Beauty' in which he puts a kingdom into a magic slumber.
Afanasyev also retells a Polish tale in which Koshchei puts others to sleep, so the Polish attestation appears in both authors.
Ralston tells the Polish tale and the Marya Morevna story without citing or quoting Afanasyev on that page, so on that passage he counts as an independent source.
Ralston's forbidden-chamber versions are footnoted to Khudyakof and Erlenvein, collectors other than Afanasyev.
Ralston's derivation of the name rests on Afanasief, whom his footnote quotes, so the etymology is counted once, not twice.

notes.text: origin: no opened page says where Koshchei comes from or who becomes one; the pages offer only the mythologists' reading of him as a personification of winter or storm (ralston1872 pp.164-167, ralston1873 p.84, afanasyev1868 pp.594-595, 603), which was not recorded as folk origin. Searched koshchei, koschei, kashchei, кощей, кощеи, кащей, безсмертный across all sources.

variants: the only people-specific telling is a Polish 'Sleeping Beauty' version (ralston1872 p.166), recorded in behavior_habitat with its people named in the clause rather than as a variant, since it differs in plot, not in description.

Interpretations of Koshchei as winter, storm or a demon of rain-clouds (ralston1872 pp.164-167, afanasyev1868 pp.594-595, 603) are mythologists' readings and are kept out of every field. The 'bony of limb' guess is in meaning only, as part of an etymology, and not in appearance.

Unread relevant pages (budget): afanasyev1868 pp.596-602 and 604 (retell the Koshchei tales; may add scene and dealing details); ralston1873 pp.85-96 and 101-108 (full texts of Marya Morevna and Koshchei the Deathless; may add scene and behaviour); ralston1872 p.373 (charm naming 'Koshchei-yadun'; would give a romanised variant); afanasyev1868 pp.430, 615, 714, 780 (passing mentions).

related: zmey-gorynych is linked because ralston1873 p.115 says names such as Koshchei admit of exchange with Zmei Goruinuich, and afanasyev1868 p.594 names Zmey Gorynych and Koshchei together as underground kings; baba-yaga because ralston1873 p.97 calls the Baba Yaga the feminine counterpart of Koshchei and the Snake.
